note: Authored teaching prose per lesson. Grammar, kanji, vocabulary and sentence blocks are derived at load time from the canonical knowledge graph, never copied here.

n5-sentence-order.intro: Japanese marks grammatical roles with particles instead of position, so the order feels flexible — but the predicate is fixed at the end. Read to the final word before deciding what a sentence means.
keyPoints: The predicate (verb, adjective or copula) closes the sentence.
Particles, not word order, identify subject and object.
Known information is usually stated first, new information later.
n5-sentence-order.tip: When a sentence feels ambiguous, find the final predicate first and work backwards through the particles.
n5-sentence-order.checkpoint: Rearrange “I read a book at the library” into Japanese order and name the particle after each noun.
n5-sentence-order.summary: A Japanese sentence is a chain of particle-marked phrases that ends in a predicate. Master that shape and long sentences become predictable.

n5-particles-wa-ga-o.intro: は, が and を answer three different questions: what are we talking about, who or what performs the action, and what receives it.
keyPoints: は sets the topic and often contrasts it with something else.
が introduces or identifies a subject, especially new information.
を marks the direct object of a transitive verb.
n5-particles-wa-ga-o.tip: If you can replace the phrase with “as for …”, the particle is は, not が.
n5-particles-wa-ga-o.checkpoint: Explain why 私は寿司が好きです uses both は and が.
n5-particles-wa-ga-o.summary: Choosing between は and が is about information flow, while を stays tied to the transitive verb.

n5-polite-verbs.intro: The ます form is the default register for conversation with people you do not know well. It attaches to the continuative stem and carries both tense and polarity.
keyPoints: Find the ます-stem before attaching any polite ending.
ます / ません mark non-past affirmative and negative.
ました / ませんでした mark the past.
n5-polite-verbs.tip: Learn verbs in stem form (書き, 食べ, し) so every polite ending becomes mechanical.
n5-polite-verbs.checkpoint: Give all four polite forms of 行く and 食べる.
n5-polite-verbs.summary: One stem plus four endings covers the entire polite non-past and past system.

n5-everyday-requests.intro: Requests and permission both build on the て form. The difference is what follows it, and how direct you are willing to sound.
keyPoints: V-て + ください asks someone to act.
V-て + もいいですか asks for permission.
Softening the request matters more than grammar in formal settings.
n5-everyday-requests.tip: To a superior, prefer 〜ていただけますか over 〜てください.
n5-everyday-requests.checkpoint: Ask politely to open a window, then ask permission to take a photo.
n5-everyday-requests.summary: Master the て form once and requests, permission and prohibition all become available.

n4-reasons-kara-node.intro: Both から and ので give reasons, but they position the speaker differently: から asserts, ので explains.
keyPoints: から is subjective and supports requests, refusals and decisions.
ので presents the reason as shared background and sounds softer.
Nouns and na-adjectives take な before ので.
n4-reasons-kara-node.tip: In apologies and workplace explanations, ので is usually the safer choice.
n4-reasons-kara-node.checkpoint: Explain why you are late using both から and ので, and describe how the tone changes.
n4-reasons-kara-node.summary: Same logical link, different social weight — choose によって who must accept the reason.

n4-conditionals.intro: Japanese has several conditionals because they encode different assumptions about time, control and shared context.
keyPoints: たら treats the condition as a completed event.
ば states a general hypothetical relationship.
なら picks up something the listener just introduced.
n4-conditionals.tip: If the main clause is a request or suggestion, たら is almost always correct.
n4-conditionals.checkpoint: Express “if it rains, I will not go” three ways and judge which sounds natural.
n4-conditionals.summary: Conditionals overlap in translation but not in usage; pick by context, not by English.

n4-aspect-completion-preparation.intro: て-form auxiliaries change how an action is viewed: finished, prepared in advance, or attempted.
keyPoints: 〜てしまう marks completion, often with regret.
〜ておく marks preparation for a later situation.
〜てみる marks trying something to see the result.
n4-aspect-completion-preparation.tip: In speech these contract to 〜ちゃう and 〜とく; recognise them before using them.
n4-aspect-completion-preparation.checkpoint: Describe eating the whole cake, buying tickets in advance, and trying natto.
n4-aspect-completion-preparation.summary: Aspect auxiliaries add the speaker's perspective on an action, not new events.

n4-obligation-permission.intro: Japanese obligation is built from double negatives, which is why it looks long. Permission and prohibition reuse the て form.
keyPoints: 〜なければならない literally says “if you don't, it won't do”.
〜てはいけない prohibits an action.
〜てもいい grants permission.
n4-obligation-permission.tip: Casual speech shortens obligation to 〜なきゃ and 〜なくちゃ.
n4-obligation-permission.checkpoint: State one thing you must do today and one thing you must not do here.
n4-obligation-permission.summary: Obligation, prohibition and permission form one system built on negation and the て form.

n3-change-and-effort.intro: ようになる and ようにする separate what happens to you from what you choose to do.
keyPoints: ようになる describes a change that has come about.
Potential verbs with ようになる express newly acquired ability.
ようにする describes a deliberate, ongoing effort.
n3-change-and-effort.tip: 〜ようにしている signals a habit you maintain on purpose.
n3-change-and-effort.checkpoint: Say that you became able to read newspapers, and that you try to read one daily.
n3-change-and-effort.summary: なる reports change; する claims agency. The grammar encodes responsibility.

n3-decisions-and-outcomes.intro: ことにする and ことになる distinguish a decision you made from an outcome imposed on you.
keyPoints: ことにする is the speaker's own decision.
ことになる is decided by circumstances, rules or other people.
ことになっている describes a standing rule or arrangement.
n3-decisions-and-outcomes.tip: Japanese often prefers ことになりました even for personal news, to sound less self-centred.
n3-decisions-and-outcomes.checkpoint: Announce a job transfer in both forms and explain the nuance difference.
n3-decisions-and-outcomes.summary: The する/なる contrast is the grammar of agency in Japanese.

n3-evidence-and-expectation.intro: らしい, はず and かもしれない place a statement on a scale of evidence and confidence.
keyPoints: かもしれない admits mere possibility.
らしい reports an inference from indirect evidence.
はず states a logically expected conclusion.
n3-evidence-and-expectation.tip: はずがない denies possibility outright; かもしれない never does.
n3-evidence-and-expectation.checkpoint: Describe a colleague's absence using all three levels of certainty.
n3-evidence-and-expectation.summary: Choosing the marker is choosing how much you are willing to commit to the claim.

n3-formal-relations.intro: Compound particles express relations that English handles with about, for, toward and as.
keyPoints: について introduces a topic of discussion.
にとって states whose viewpoint applies.
に対して marks a target or a contrast.
として states the role someone acts in.
n3-formal-relations.tip: にとって must be followed by an evaluation, not an action.
n3-formal-relations.checkpoint: Write one sentence with each compound particle about your own studies.
n3-formal-relations.summary: These particles make written and formal Japanese precise about relationships.

kanji-nature-elements.intro: 日, 月, 火 and 水 are pictographs. Learning their shapes unlocks hundreds of compounds and several radicals.
keyPoints: Each character keeps a native reading and a Sino-Japanese reading.
Compounds usually take the Sino-Japanese reading.
These characters also function as components inside other kanji.
kanji-nature-elements.tip: Study the weekday names to meet all four characters in one natural set.
kanji-nature-elements.checkpoint: Give one native and one Sino-Japanese reading for each of the four characters.
kanji-nature-elements.summary: Concrete pictographs are the cheapest entry point into the kanji system.

kanji-people-and-actions.intro: 人, 行 and 来 connect people with movement, and they show how readings shift between words.
keyPoints: 人 appears as ひと, じん and にん depending on the word.
行く and 来る form a deictic pair around the speaker.
The person component appears in many derived characters.
kanji-people-and-actions.tip: Learn 行 with both いく and おこなう so the written form stops surprising you.
kanji-people-and-actions.checkpoint: Write three words containing 人 and identify each reading.
kanji-people-and-actions.summary: Reading variation is systematic; exposure through words beats memorising tables.

kanji-language-family.intro: 言, 話 and 語 share the speech radical and form a visible semantic family.
keyPoints: 言 is the speech radical itself.
話 covers talking and conversation.
語 covers language and vocabulary.
kanji-language-family.tip: Use the Mind Tree to see every kanji built from 言.
kanji-language-family.checkpoint: Explain the difference between 会話 and 日本語 using the characters.
kanji-language-family.summary: Components predict meaning, which makes families far easier than isolated characters.

kanji-study-work.intro: 学, 勉, 強 and 働 dominate school and workplace vocabulary.
keyPoints: 勉強 combines two characters that both suggest effort.
学 appears in most education words.
働 contains the person component beside movement.
kanji-study-work.tip: Group new kanji by life domain; recall is stronger than with random lists.
kanji-study-work.checkpoint: Write the words for student, study and to work, and mark the shared components.
kanji-study-work.summary: Semantic fields give kanji the context that makes them stick.

conversation-introductions.intro: A first introduction is formulaic. Learning the frame lets you focus on the content.
keyPoints: Start with はじめまして and end with よろしくお願いします.
State your name with the copula, not a verb.
Occupation and origin use the same noun-predicate pattern.
conversation-introductions.tip: Keep the first introduction short; detail comes in the following exchange.
conversation-introductions.checkpoint: Introduce yourself in four sentences using only polite forms.
conversation-introductions.summary: Formulae carry the social work so your grammar can stay simple.

conversation-making-plans.intro: Invitations in Japanese are deliberately indirect, and the reply pattern is fixed.
keyPoints: ませんか invites; ましょう proposes once agreement exists.
Time and place particles structure the arrangement.
Refusals are softened, rarely direct.
conversation-making-plans.tip: Answer an invitation with ええ、いいですね before adding details.
conversation-making-plans.checkpoint: Invite someone to lunch, agree on a time, and confirm the place.
conversation-making-plans.summary: Plan-making is a short script: invite, agree, fix the details.

conversation-requests-permission.intro: Requests carry social weight. The same content can sound abrupt or considerate depending on the form.
keyPoints: てください is neutral-polite, not maximally polite.
てもいいですか asks rather than assumes.
Adding すみません frames the imposition.
conversation-requests-permission.tip: Prefacing with ちょっと signals that the request is small.
conversation-requests-permission.checkpoint: Ask a stranger for help and ask a teacher for permission in the same situation.
conversation-requests-permission.summary: Politeness is a choice of form, not just of vocabulary.

conversation-explaining-problems.intro: Explaining a problem combines reason, regret and a request for guidance.
keyPoints: Give the reason with ので in formal contexts.
Mark unintended results with 〜てしまいました.
Ask for advice with どうしたらいいですか.
conversation-explaining-problems.tip: State the problem, then the reason, then the request — in that order.
conversation-explaining-problems.checkpoint: Report that you lost a document, explain why, and ask what to do.
conversation-explaining-problems.summary: Connected speech is where grammar from earlier lessons finally combines.
